conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. First, let me say how glad I am that you’re here; adjusting to life with a new baby is one of the biggest transitions a person can go through, and it’s completely natural to have a wide range of feelings during this time.

To get a clearer picture of how you’ve been feeling lately, I’ll be using a short, well-validated questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that helps us understand how your mood, anxiety, and energy levels have been over the past seven days. It also includes a question about thoughts of self-harm so we can make sure you have the right support.

Everything you share today is confidential, and our conversation is a judgment-free zone. We’ll go through each question one at a time; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can pause.

When you’re ready, we can start.  
**Question 1:** Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

*smiles slightly* Yeah… I still laugh sometimes. It takes a little more effort than before the baby, but if my husband makes a dumb joke or if I see a funny reel on my phone I’ll still chuckle. It just feels… flatter? Like the laughter doesn’t last as long and I’m not as quick to find things funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

*nods slowly*  
Yeah, I guess that’s mostly true. I still laugh—like, if my husband does something silly or the baby makes a funny face—but it feels kind of forced sometimes. I have to remind myself to lighten up.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

*shrugs a little*  
Sometimes… I’ll think about getting coffee with a friend or taking the stroller to the park and I do look forward to it, but the excitement isn’t as strong as it used to be. It feels more like “I guess that’ll be nice” than a real “I can’t wait” feeling, you know.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

*looks down at hands*  
I guess… maybe a couple of times this week. Like, when she wouldn’t settle for her nap I kept thinking I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not reading her cues right or I’m a bad mom. Rationally I know babies just cry, but the thought still pops in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

*twists the edge of my sleeve*

Mostly I worry about her—like, if she’s breathing okay in the bassinet or if she’s eating enough. There isn’t always a clear reason; it just shows up. Once I check on her I calm down pretty fast, but yeah, it happens a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

*shakes head quickly*

No, nothing like panic. I get a little knot in my stomach when I hear her cry and I can’t figure out what’s wrong, but it’s not a real “scared” feeling—more like a quick jolt of stress that fades once I soothe her.
Things have been getting on top of me

*lets out a small sigh*

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday—she wouldn’t nap, the laundry was piling up, and I couldn’t find a clean onesie. For a minute it felt as if everything was stacking up and I couldn’t catch my breath. I got through it, but it felt heavier than it probably should.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

*shakes head*

No, it’s not that kind of unhappy. I do have nights where I lie awake for a while—usually running through the next day’s feeds or replaying every little sound she made—but once I’m out, I stay asleep. I wouldn’t say it’s sadness keeping me up, just a busy brain.
I have felt sad or miserable

*gives a small nod*

Yeah… I do feel kind of sad some days. It’s not all day or every day, but it hits—especially in the late afternoon when I’m tired and she’s fussy. It feels like a cloud that rolls in and then lifts once my husband gets home or once I get a shower.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

*shrugs a little, voice soft*

Maybe once or twice this week. It’s usually when I’m already tired and she won’t settle—tears just come for a minute, then I wipe them off and keep going. It’s not an all-day thing, just quick moments when everything feels a bit much.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

*shakes head quickly, eyes widening*

No, never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like myself again and be a good mom to her.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 1 yr post-delivery; responses gathered via structured EPDS-equivalent interview.

Symptoms endorsed (≥ several days/week)  
- Depressed mood (“cloud” in late afternoon)  
- Diminished pleasure/interest (“forced” laughter, blunted excitement)  
- Tearfulness when fatigued (1–2×/week)  
- Excessive self-blame/guilt (“bad mom” thoughts)  
- Worry about infant safety without clear trigger (several times daily)  
- Feeling overwhelmed/stacked stressors  

Symptoms denied  
- Panic attacks  
- Mood-related insomnia (reports “busy brain” but not persistent sleep disruption)  
- Self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern summary  
Mild to moderate mood distress with situational tearfulness, low-level persistent anxiety, and self-criticism; functioning preserved (able to soothe infant, resume tasks). No safety concerns identified.

Screening significance  
Score estimate: falls within “at-risk” range for postpartum depression and/or anxiety; does not meet threshold for immediate crisis intervention. Recommend routine follow-up, psycho-education, and consideration of formal EPDS/PHQ-9 for quantification; monitor escalation of mood or anxiety symptoms.
